--- title: "Accuracy and speed" --- `stateMINT` stands in for `malariasimulation`, so the question that decides whether it can be used is how closely it reproduces the simulator on parameter sets it was never trained on. We compare the two on the held-out split, first as trajectories and then as a distribution of error, and we finish by measuring what a prediction costs. ## The held-out split The emulator was trained on a library of `malariasimulation` runs, split by parameter set into 70% training, 15% validation and 15% test. The figures below use the test split only, taken from the split file that shipped with the trained weights, so every trajectory belongs to a parameter set the model never saw in any epoch. ::: {#f45f3328 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` held-out runs 1,954 time points 306,778 ``` ::: ::: ## Trajectories Five held-out runs spanning the 10th to the 90th percentile of EIR are plotted below, with the simulator drawn as a dashed white line over the emulator's solid blue one. ::: {#22666a0e .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} panels = sorted(traj["panel"].unique()) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(panels), figsize=(14.5, 3.1), sharey=True) for ax, p in zip(axes, panels): d = traj[traj["panel"] == p] ax.plot(d["years_from_campaign"], d["emulator"], color="#3987e5", lw=2.6, label="stateMINT", zorder=2) ax.plot(d["years_from_campaign"], d["truth"], color="#ffffff", lw=1.5, ls=(0, (4, 2.6)), label="malariasimulation", zorder=3) ax.axvline(0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=0.9, alpha=0.6, zorder=1) ax.set_title(f"EIR {d['eir'].iloc[0]:g}", fontsize=9.5) ax.set_xlabel("years from campaign") axes[0].set_ylabel("prevalence") axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="best") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Out-of-sample prevalence under five held-out parameter sets. The dashed white line is malariasimulation and the solid blue line is stateMINT.](validation_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){fig-alt='Five panels of prevalence over time. In each, the emulator\'s solid coloured line lies almost exactly under the simulator\'s dashed white ground-truth line, before and after the campaign.'} ::: ::: Because the truth is dashed over the top of the emulator, any disagreement between the two would appear as the white line separating from the blue. The two stay close across all five panels, and the emulator tracks the pre-campaign equilibrium, the drop when the intervention lands, and the shape of the recovery, including the sharp annual oscillation of the strongly seasonal setting in the right-hand panel. Note that the simulator traces are noisy. An individual-based model produces a stochastic trajectory and the emulator predicts the smooth expectation through it, so part of the residual here is the simulator's own Monte Carlo noise rather than emulator error. ## Pipeline error and emulator error The figure above gives the emulator the EIR the simulator itself was run at. A user does not have that number and has to estimate it from a prevalence survey, so the error they see is the error of the whole chain rather than of the emulator alone. To separate the two we plot three held-out parameter sets with both paths drawn. The white line is `malariasimulation`, averaged over the stochastic runs drawn in grey behind it. The red line is the full pipeline, which starts from the measured year-9 prevalence and inverts it to an EIR with `estimint` before running `stateMINT` forward. The green dashed line is `stateMINT` given the simulator's own EIR. The gap between green and white is therefore the cost of the emulation, while the gap between red and green is the cost of the inversion. ::: {#29e4b9fb .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} cases = [16, 20, 27] fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(13.5, 6.0), sharex=True) for col, cid in enumerate(cases): truth_panel(axes[0, col], cid, "prevalence") truth_panel(axes[1, col], cid, "cases") axes[0, col].set_title(truth_title(cid), fontsize=9) axes[1, col].set_xlabel("years from campaign") axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("prevalence") axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("cases per 1000 per day") axes[0, 0].plot([], [], color=TRUTH, lw=3.4, label="malariasimulation") axes[0, 0].plot([], [], color=PIPELINE, lw=1.8, label="pipeline") axes[0, 0].plot([], [], color=EMULATOR, lw=1.5, ls=(0, (4, 2.6)), label="emulator at true EIR") axes[0, 0].legend(fontsize=7.5, loc="best") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Three held-out parameter sets. White is malariasimulation averaged over the grey stochastic runs, red is the full pipeline from a measured prevalence, and green dashed is the emulator given the simulator's own EIR.](validation_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){fig-alt='Two rows of three panels, prevalence above and clinical cases below. In each panel the red pipeline line and the green dashed emulator line both track the white simulator average closely, within the spread of the grey individual runs.'} ::: ::: Each panel fails in a different way, and the two failures are worth telling apart. In the left panel all three lines coincide, which is the case where the inversion recovers the EIR and the emulator reproduces the simulator. In the middle panel the red line runs above the white one while the green line stays on it, because `estimint` estimated an EIR of 12.5 against a true 11.8 and the emulator was then run forward from a transmission intensity that was too high. In the right panel red and green coincide with each other but both sit slightly below the simulator once the campaign lands, so there the residual belongs to the emulator rather than to the inversion. ::: {#e7ef2e4d .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
setting true EIR estimated EIR MAE, emulator MAE, pipeline
Seasonal, ITN Only, Low EIR, Low dn0 1.98 1.99 0.0039 0.0037
Perennial, IRS Only, Mid EIR 11.78 12.50 0.0025 0.0070
Perennial, ITN+IRS, Low EIR, Low dn0 1.95 1.95 0.0055 0.0056
``` ::: ::: The middle setting carries a pipeline error roughly three times its emulator error, and the other two carry pipeline and emulator errors that are the same size. This is the general shape of the stack. Where the inversion is accurate the emulator sets the floor on the error, and where the inversion is not, it dominates, which is why the prevalence survey a run starts from matters more to the answer than the emulator does. ## Error on the held-out set ::: {#416e48d9 .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
prevalence
Mean absolute error 0.0044
Median absolute error 0.0032
90th percentile of MAE 0.0081
Worst run 0.0568
RMSE 0.0056
Mean bias -0.00037
R² 0.99877
``` ::: ::: These numbers are in prevalence units, so a mean absolute error of 0.0044 means the emulator's prevalence is typically within about 0.4 percentage points of the simulator's, and a run at 30% prevalence is reproduced somewhere between roughly 29.6% and 30.4%. The mean bias of about −0.0004 says the emulator is not systematically high or low. ::: {#831f6b9f .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.2)) ax.hist(run_mae["mae"], bins=60, color="#199e70", edgecolor="none") ax.axvline(summary["mae_median"], color="#e66767", lw=1.6, label=f"median {summary['mae_median']:.4f}") ax.axvline(summary["mae_p90"], color="#c98500", lw=1.6, ls="--", label=f"90th pct {summary['mae_p90']:.4f}") ax.set_xlabel("mean absolute error, per held-out run") ax.set_ylabel("runs") ax.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Distribution of per-run mean absolute error across the held-out split.](validation_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){fig-alt='A histogram of per-run mean absolute error, concentrated near zero with a short right tail.'} ::: ::: The distribution is tight and right-skewed, and the worst single run in the held-out set is off by about 0.057, which is under six percentage points of prevalence. That error sets the resolution of any comparison between campaigns. Differences smaller than about half a percentage point of prevalence sit inside the emulator's own error and should not be read as real. ## Speed A `malariasimulation` run over the same 12 simulated years takes minutes, while the emulator is a single forward pass. ::: {#cc7aaa38 .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
batch size total (ms) per scenario (ms)
1 17.780000 17.780000
8 90.950000 11.370000
32 257.850000 8.060000
128 904.940000 7.070000
512 3254.340000 6.360000
2048 12474.470000 6.090000
``` ::: ::: On CPU a single isolated call costs more per scenario than a batched one, and most of that difference is fixed dispatch overhead rather than computation. Amortised across a batch the cost settles at a few milliseconds per scenario, so passing a list to `predict` or `run_scenarios` is markedly cheaper than looping over it, which is why the API takes a list. On a GPU the same forward pass is roughly six times faster again (measured on an NVIDIA L40S). For a scenario grid the CPU is entirely adequate, and the GPU matters when you are sweeping thousands of parameter sets. A campaign comparison that would once have been a batch job on a cluster now runs inside a loop, or behind a web form, at interactive speed. ## See also What is actually inside the emulator is described in [The models](models.qmd), and the download, the compilation and the GPU extra in [Performance and caching](../05-statemint/performance.qmd). Please see [Trajectories and cases](../06-scenarios/comparing.qmd) for the speed put to use.
